archetype.name: Playoff Team (defense-first)
archetype.definition: Seattle wins with a top-three defense and strong special teams, while a middling, run-heavy offense with an unsettled quarterback spot does just enough.

report.headline: An elite defense carrying a Lock-led offense that still can't run the ball.
report.take:
This is the 2025 Seahawks' identity carried forward. Last year Macdonald's defense finished first in EPA allowed and first in points allowed on the way to 14 wins. Four games into 2026 it is third in EPA allowed, second in success rate allowed and first in yards allowed at 247.3 per game. The 3-1 record is mostly earned: wins over expected sit at just 0.23, the point differential is +8 a game, and net EPA ranks 8th. Unlike last year's +3.29 luck number, nothing here is inflated by close-game fortune.

The defense has a clear shape. It erases the deep ball (deep EPA allowed ranks 2nd, explosive pass rate allowed 3rd), hits the quarterback often (hit rate 4th) and tackles well (missed-tackle rate 4th). The price is underneath: short-pass EPA allowed ranks 28th, so offenses can move the ball in small chunks, and the red-zone TD rate allowed is 22nd. That explains why the No. 1 yardage defense ranks only 5th in points allowed. The offense is a decent passing team (pass EPA 10th) hitched to a bad run game. Rush EPA ranks 26th, stuff rate 27th, and short-yardage conversion 31st. Even so, the team runs more than expected (pass rate over expected is 25th).

The numbers hide two things. First, the defense has not yet faced a good offense. NE, ARI, WAS and LAC rank 22nd, 17th, 21st and 31st in offensive EPA today. The one that scored 33 did it with help from three Seattle turnovers. Second, the rushing yardage flatters the ground game. The 162 yards at Arizona came with -7.1 rush EPA, and the 138 against the Chargers with -3.5. That is game-script volume while protecting leads, not efficiency. Meanwhile Drew Lock's pass EPA has dropped across his three starts, from 16.1 to 5.0 to -5.2. The win over LAC came from four takeaways, not offense. The usage table credits Darnold with 560 yards in three appearances against Lock's 422 in two. Who is really running this offense is less settled than the start list suggests.

Going forward, the defense is the most bankable thing on the roster. Two straight seasons of top-three EPA allowed under the same coach is not noise. The offense is the variable. With Charbonnet still on PUP and Jadarian Price on IR, the backfield is down to Emanuel Wilson and George Holani. That makes improvement in the run game unlikely, so Seattle will go as far as its passing game and its takeaway rate allow.

strengths.title: Top-three defense with real pedigree
strengths.body: Seattle ranks 3rd in EPA allowed and 2nd in success rate allowed, following a 2025 in which it was 1st. That continuity under the same staff says the scheme travels from year to year and isn't a four-game fluke. The caveat is that every offense it has faced ranks 17th or worse, so the ceiling is still unproven.

strengths.title: Nothing gets behind this secondary
strengths.body: Deep-pass EPA allowed is -0.516, 2nd in the league, and the explosive pass rate allowed is 3rd. Pair that with a 4th-ranked hit rate and opponents can't take shots without the quarterback getting hit. This is a structural feature of the coverage and should hold up against better offenses.

strengths.title: Takeaways and special teams swing games
strengths.body: Seven takeaways (6th) and special-teams EPA ranked 5th have produced hidden yardage. The three takeaways against New England and four against the Chargers were the difference in both wins. Special teams tends to be stable, but takeaway bursts like these come and go.

concerns.title: A run game that can't move
concerns.body: Rush EPA ranks 26th and the stuff rate 27th, and Seattle converts only 22.2% in short yardage (31st). With the line averaging 2.29 yards before contact, the backs are fighting from behind the line. Charbonnet on PUP and Price on IR make a fix unlikely, yet the team keeps calling runs at a below-expected pass rate. That is a real flaw, not a game-script artifact.

concerns.title: Lock's trajectory and ball security
concerns.body: Across Lock's three starts, pass EPA went from 16.1 against a 27th-ranked defense to -5.2 against the Chargers. In between came a three-turnover loss in Washington despite 393 passing yards. Protection is part of the story: the pressure rate allowed ranks 24th and time to throw is among the longest in the league. Expect this to persist without a better plan to get the ball out.

concerns.title: Penalties and a soft underbelly
concerns.body: Seattle is drawing 8.8 flags a game (25th), including 150 penalty yards against the Chargers. On defense, short-pass EPA allowed ranks 28th and the red-zone TD rate allowed ranks 22nd. These are the leaks that let mediocre offenses hang 23 and 33 points. Penalties are fixable; the short-pass softness looks like a cost of the deep-first coverage.

trend.note: The defense has been steady all month. The offense swung from a 31-7 rout to a turnover-driven 33-31 loss to a win carried entirely by four takeaways, and passing efficiency has fallen across Lock's three starts.

nextGame.headline: First real test: Seattle's defense meets the league's best offense.
nextGame.body:
San Francisco is the No. 1 offense by EPA, No. 1 in pass EPA and No. 1 in success rate. It also leads the league in pass protection: a 9.8% pressure rate and zero sacks allowed. That neutralizes Seattle's best weapon, its pass rush. The 49ers' short, timing-based passing game also aims right at Seattle's weak spot, short-pass defense. The other side is more promising for Seattle. The SF defense is only 14th in EPA, 27th in hit rate and 24th on third downs. Its 16 points allowed per game lean on a 5th-ranked red-zone TD rate and a 4-0 record built partly on 1.43 wins over expected.

Availability tilts toward Seattle. San Francisco is without Nick Bosa and DT James Thompson Jr., which strips an already weak rush. Starting safety Marques Sigle (88% of snaps) is doubtful with a multi-week high-ankle sprain, and fullback Kyle Juszczyk is doubtful too. For Seattle, Leonard Williams (70% snaps) is expected to play through his ankle. The backfield remains thin with Charbonnet still on PUP and Price on IR. The market has priced this as Seattle -2.5, which looks about right.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's pass rush vs. SF's wall
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's 4th-ranked hit rate meets a line that has allowed the fewest pressures and no sacks. If the rush can't get home, Seattle's deep-ball defense still holds, but the short-area softness becomes the battleground. This is the clearest stress test of the defense so far.

keyMatchups.title: Lock against a toothless rush
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's protection has been a problem, but SF's hit rate ranks 27th and it is missing Bosa and Thompson. This is the cleanest pocket Lock is likely to see. San Francisco limits explosives (2nd in explosive pass rate allowed), so Seattle has to win on third down, where SF ranks 24th.

keyMatchups.title: Red zone finishing on both ends
keyMatchups.body: Seattle allows TDs on 66.7% of red-zone trips, while SF's defense holds opponents to 45.5%. In a game between two defenses that bend more than they break, field goals versus touchdowns likely decide it.

nextGame.watch: Whether Seattle can pressure Purdy at all without blitzing into the short throws its coverage already struggles with.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense should stay top-five. It has the pedigree, the tackling and the deep-coverage profile to hold up. Some regression is likely as the schedule stiffens, with KC, CHI, SF twice counting the division and the Rams' 4th-ranked defense twice. The takeaway pace will also cool. The offense projects as roughly league-average: a competent passing game dragged down by a run game that lacks healthy backs until Charbonnet and Price return. The Week 3 three-turnover game is the downside case if the quarterback play keeps sliding.

The record isn't inflated, so there is little luck to give back, but there isn't much margin either. The schedule includes three games against defenses ranked 5th or better, plus a road trip to the Raiders' 2nd-ranked unit. A 10-12 win range fits a team with this defense and this offense. The division title likely hinges on the two SF games against a 49ers team whose 4-0 record carries some close-game fortune.
swingFactors: Quarterback stability and Lock's turnover rate
Charbonnet and Price returning to fix the run game
Whether the defense holds up against top-10 offenses

bets.reason: Both teams allow fewer than 19 points a game, and Seattle's run-heavy approach shortens games. The total is higher than any of Seattle's four lines this year (40.5 to 44.5). Blending each offense's scoring with the other defense's points allowed lands closer to 45 than 47.5.

confidence.note: Four games, a defense untested against good offenses, and an unsettled QB split.
